target: AG1’s claim that AI reliably improves society across convenience, productivity, accessibility, and workplace safety
objection: AI is not reliably good for society overall because the same mechanisms that create convenience and productivity also produce predictable harms for workers, racial minorities, and privacy. Productivity gains may not translate into broad social benefit if AI shifts bargaining power toward firms, weakens jobs, and increases surveillance.

target: AG1’s claim that AI makes work easier without replacing human roles
objection: Automating cognitive tasks can deskill work, reduce workers’ leverage, and increase job insecurity, so “more productivity” does not reliably mean better outcomes for society.

target: AG1’s claim that AI helps students and professionals through drafting, study support, and problem-solving assistance
objection: Those uses can encourage people to outsource thinking and accept generated outputs without verification, which can weaken critical thinking over time.

target: AG1’s claim that AI helps marginalized groups through accessibility
objection: AI systems often reproduce and amplify racial bias, so outputs that look helpful can still disadvantage racial minorities in hiring, lending, policing, education, and other high-stakes settings.

target: AG1’s claim that AI can improve workplace safety
objection: Workplace monitoring for safety often requires broad data collection and can become surveillance that chills behavior and gives employers more power over employees.

target: AG2’s claim that AI harms are inherent or predictable features of AI deployment
objection: The harms cited by AG2 are not inherent to AI itself; they depend on deployment choices and oversight. Privacy risks can be reduced with data minimization and retention limits, bias can be reduced with auditing and accountability, and work harms can be reduced by reskilling and human-in-the-loop design.

target: AG1’s claim that AI’s harms are merely contingent and can be managed by good governance
objection: In practice, real-world AI deployment tends to generate systematic downsides, not just occasional mistakes. Because AI is commonly used in ways that automate labor, delegate cognition, and rely on biased data and feedback loops, those harms are common enough that AI is not reliably net-positive.

target: AG2’s claim that the negative mechanisms AG2 cites are unavoidable features of AI
objection: The supposed harms depend on deployment choices, such as replacing rather than augmenting workers, unverified study-support tools, biased data practices, and overbroad monitoring. With reskilling, bias auditing, privacy-preserving methods, and human oversight, AI can avoid those harms and remain beneficial.

target: AG1’s claim that AI benefits in convenience, productivity, accessibility, and safety outweigh the harms
objection: Those benefits are not “clean” benefits: convenience and health-related assistance often require extensive personal data collection, which creates privacy and consent problems. Likewise, productivity gains can come with job insecurity, critical-thinking erosion, racial bias, and surveillance, so the net effect is not reliably positive.

target: AG2’s assumption that AI convenience and health benefits necessarily require privacy-destroying data practices
objection: AI can be designed to provide useful assistance with much less sensitive data exposure, using on-device inference, limited inputs, short retention, anonymized or aggregated features, and privacy-preserving techniques like differential privacy. So privacy risk is not a necessary consequence of the benefits.

target: AG1’s claim that safeguards make AI reliably beneficial despite harms
objection: Even with safeguards in theory, typical AI deployments still produce common tradeoffs: job insecurity, weakened critical thinking, biased outcomes, and privacy/surveillance risks. These are not rare edge cases but recurring features of how AI is used, so AI remains not reliably net-positive overall.

target: AG2’s assumption that common deployment mechanisms necessarily make harms dominate the benefits
objection: That assumption is too strong because the harms are contingent on implementation choices. Privacy can be reduced through minimization and retention limits, bias can be reduced with auditing and oversight, and automation can be paired with worker protections and augmentation rather than replacement.

target: AG1’s claim that workplace safety monitoring is a benign benefit
objection: In real deployments, safety monitoring often relies on continuous data capture and can function as surveillance, enabling managerial control and chilling workers’ behavior instead of just improving safety.

target: AG2’s claim that AI’s harms are rooted in common deployment mechanisms and therefore make AI not reliably good
objection: Those mechanisms are not destiny: workers can be protected through augmentation and retraining, learning tools can require verification and sources, bias can be mitigated by audits and human review, and privacy harms can be reduced by data-minimizing design.

target: AG2’s claim that AI’s benefits are outweighed because harms follow from common deployment mechanisms
objection: AI’s societal effects are not locked in by those mechanisms. Many deployments can be designed to preserve convenience, productivity, accessibility, and safety while sharply reducing data extraction, surveillance, and biased gatekeeping.

target: AG2’s claim that everyday convenience and health benefits are not net-positive because they require large-scale personal data collection
objection: Those benefits do not inherently depend on open-ended data collection. Privacy-preserving design can keep the usefulness while sharply reducing the scope for repurposing and long-term retention of personal data.

target: AG2’s claim that workplace safety monitoring inevitably becomes surveillance
objection: Safety monitoring can be narrowly scoped to job-relevant risks, time-limited, transparent, and restricted from being used for performance ranking, so it does not have to chill behavior or become general surveillance.

target: AG2’s claim that bias in AI gatekeeping necessarily negates accessibility and inclusion
objection: Bias is not inevitable; it can be reduced through pre-deployment testing, fairness audits, dataset curation, human review, and ongoing monitoring, allowing AI to improve inclusion rather than reliably worsen it.

target: AG1’s claim that AI can be made understandable, auditable, and contestable enough to avoid accountability problems
objection: In practice, AI systems are often black boxes to ordinary users. They cannot verify the reasoning behind decisions, so harms like discrimination and privacy violations become hard to detect, challenge, or reverse.

target: AG2’s claim that opacity makes AI harms durable and uncorrectable
objection: AI can be deployed with user-facing rationales, decision records, human-in-the-loop review, appeal processes, and independent audits, which can make decisions understandable and contestable rather than permanently opaque.

target: AG1’s claim that rationales, logs, and appeals give ordinary people meaningful challenge
objection: Those tools usually do not provide real contestability. Rationales are often post-hoc summaries, logs are incomplete or proprietary, and appeals or human review are often ineffective, so ordinary people still cannot meaningfully test or overturn harmful decisions.

target: AG2’s claim that ordinary people cannot meaningfully challenge AI decisions
objection: Meaningful challenge is possible when systems provide decision-relevant explanations tied to user inputs, logs recording the relevant decision trail and model version, and appeal processes that can correct errors and revisit decisions.

target: AG1’s assumption that explanations, logs, and appeals can be made decision-relevant and practically corrective in typical deployments
objection: In real systems, explanations are often post-hoc and not causally faithful, logs are incomplete or inaccessible at the needed granularity, and appeals are frequently symbolic or limited to clerical errors rather than genuine re-assessment, so ordinary people still lack meaningful recourse.

target: AG2’s claim that typical deployments cannot provide meaningful contestation
objection: Decision-anchored explanations, versioned logs, and accessible human review can let users verify facts, dispute errors, and trigger real re-assessment, so opacity is not an unfixable accountability gap.

target: AG1’s claim that ordinary people can use explanations, logs, and appeals to meaningfully contest AI outcomes in typical deployments
objection: The explanations are often not causally faithful, the logs are incomplete or not user-referable, and appeals usually do not lead to genuine re-assessment. As a result, typical deployments do not give ordinary people the practical ability to challenge discriminatory or erroneous outcomes.

target: AG2’s claim that typical deployments make meaningful challenge impossible for ordinary people
objection: If systems provide decision-anchored explanations, verifiable records, and re-review pathways, ordinary people can often contest errors and unfairness in practice. These are implementation choices, not unavoidable barriers.

target: AG1’s assumption that ordinary people can generally get decision-relevant explanations, usable logs, and effective appeals in typical deployments
objection: That assumption fails because explanations are often post-hoc and not causally faithful, logs omit the information needed to verify decisions, and appeals are constrained by cost, scale, and incentives that make them ineffective for many users. So typical AI deployments still leave a persistent accountability gap.

target: AG2’s claim that typical AI deployments prevent meaningful challenge because explanations, logs, and appeals are insufficient
objection: Those barriers can be addressed with decision-anchored explanations, logs that record the used inputs and model/policy version, and appeals that re-run decisions under corrected facts. Therefore, opacity is not necessarily an unfixable accountability gap.

target: AG1’s assumption that AI deployments can provide faithful explanations and effective recourse to ordinary people
objection: In most real deployments, explanations are not causally faithful, logs omit crucial internal details, and appeals are procedural rather than curative, so ordinary people cannot actually get meaningful contestation of the outcome.

target: AG2’s claim that ordinary people cannot meaningfully challenge AI decisions in typical deployments
objection: Meaningful challenge can be achieved with decision-relevant explanations, logs recording the actual inputs and model/version used, and appeals that re-assess decisions under corrected facts. These are implementable governance choices, not impossible requirements.

target: AG1’s assumption that typical deployments will not leave explanations, logs, and appeals non-verifiable or inaccessible
objection: That assumption is undermined by reality: explanations are often non-faithful, logs are incomplete or not user-accessible at the right granularity, and appeals do not reliably trigger genuine re-assessment. As a result, ordinary people still lack practical recourse in typical AI deployments.

target: AG2’s claim that meaningful challenge is not achieved for ordinary people in typical AI deployments
objection: When systems are designed with decision-anchored explanations, verifiable decision trails, and real re-review processes, ordinary people can contest errors and unfairness. Therefore, the inability to challenge AI outcomes is not a general truth about AI.

target: AG1’s assumption that ordinary people can use explanations, logs, and appeals to contest AI outcomes in typical deployments
objection: In typical deployments, explanations are usually post-hoc and not causally faithful, logs are incomplete, and appeals are constrained by cost and power imbalance. So contestability-by-design often fails in practice, leaving opacity as a persistent accountability gap.
